After passing through Toyama Electric (富山電気), it was renamed Nihonkai Electric in 1928 (Shōwa 3). It supplied electricity to most of Toyama Prefecture (excluding the area around Takaoka City) and the Noto region of Ishikawa Prefecture, and also operated a city gas supply business within Toyama City.
In 1941 (Shōwa 16), through the consolidation by new establishment of a total of 12 electric power companies in the Hokuriku region centered on Nihonkai Electric, it became Hokuriku Gōdō Electric, and the following year it was integrated into Hokuriku Haiden (Hokuriku Power Distribution), the predecessor of Hokuriku Electric Power, in accordance with the Electricity Distribution Control Ordinance. During this period, the gas business was split off and, after reorganization, transferred to Nihonkai Gas.

章节.概要:
Nihonkai Electric Co., Ltd. was a power company whose supply area covered most of Toyama Prefecture and half of the Noto region of Ishikawa Prefecture within the general transmission and distribution service area of Hokuriku Electric Power Transmission & Distribution (Hokuriku Electric Power Group), and it was the operator representing the electric power industry of the Hokuriku region in the prewar period. Its head office was in Toyama City. It was established in 1898 (Meiji 31) as "Toyama Electric Light Co., Ltd. (富山電燈株式會社)" and began operations the following year, 1899 (Meiji 32). It was the first electric power business in the three Hokuriku prefectures (in Niigata Prefecture, Niigata Electric Light had already begun operations in Niigata City in 1898). In 1907 (Meiji 40) it changed its name to "Toyama Electric Co., Ltd. (富山電氣株式會社)". In the 1920s it expanded outside Toyama Prefecture through mergers with neighboring operators, and taking that opportunity it changed its company name to "Nihonkai Electric Co., Ltd. (日本海電氣株式會社)" in 1928 (Shōwa 3). It was a company established and managed by influential figures in the local Toyama business community, and was unremarkable in terms of capital.
Its service area included the industrial zones of Fushiki Port and Toyama Port, and its business centered on large-lot power supply—supplying cheap electricity generated by hydroelectric power to large factories. The scale of its large-lot supply was top-class among the three Hokuriku prefectures, and as of the late 1930s it was second only to Nihon Denryoku (Japan Electric Power), a major industry player that also supplied the Kansai region. Unlike Nihon Denryoku, which focused on power supply, its lighting supply was also large-scale, and its number of installed electric lights was the largest among operators in the three Hokuriku prefectures. In addition, within Toyama City it operated a city gas supply business from 1913 (Taishō 2). The gas business was small compared with the electricity supply business; in the second-half settlement of accounts for 1938, gas division revenue accounted for only 1% of total revenue, smaller even than interest and dividend income. That interest and dividend income came from numerous investments, and its affiliated companies included Kurobe River Electric Power, a joint-venture power company with Denki Kagaku Kōgyō (present-day Denka), and Toyama Electric Building, the company operating its head office building.
In 1941 (Shōwa 16), it participated in the consolidation of 12 major electric power companies in the three Hokuriku prefectures and was dissolved upon the establishment of the new company Hokuriku Gōdō Electric. Of Nihonkai Electric's businesses, the electric power business was taken over the following year by Hokuriku Haiden (with some power stations going to Nihon Hassōden), newly established under the Electricity Distribution Control Ordinance. The investment division and gas business division were spun off from Hokuriku Haiden as Nihonkai Sangyō, but this was dissolved after one year, and only the gas business was inherited by Nihonkai Gas.
章节.沿革:
=== Establishment and Opening of Toyama Electric Light ===
In May 1894 (Meiji 27), an exhibition called the "Toyama Municipal Industrial Promotion Exposition" was held at the Toyama Prefectural Products Display Hall beside Hie Shrine in Toyama City. On that occasion, Kōkichi Micata and others in the city donated 545 yen, invited engineers from Tokyo Electric Light, and lit one arc lamp and many incandescent lamps at the venue. This is regarded, albeit temporarily, as the first electric lighting in Toyama City. At the time in Toyama, andon paper lanterns were the mainstream form of lighting and even oil lamps were little used, so the bright electric lights reportedly drew large numbers of onlookers.
Entering the period after the First Sino-Japanese War, the electric light business plan was gradually made concrete by Kanaoka Matazaemon, a locally elected member of the House of Representatives and a drug merchant. Based on the investigation and proposal of Kōkichi Micata, a plan was decided to carry out hydroelectric generation using the Ōkubo irrigation canal, which drew water from the Jinzū River, and in March 1896 (Meiji 29) engineers were invited and a concrete plan was fixed. The promoters who gathered for the plan were influential figures in the city, mainly those connected to the patent-medicine trade that was Toyama's local industry; the list included Kanaoka, the drug merchant Nakada Seibei, the medicine merchants Micata Rinzō and Micata Hyōzō (Kōkichi's father), and the dry-goods merchants Makino Heigorō and Sekino Zenjirō. On November 23, 1897 (Meiji 30), an inaugural general meeting was held as "Toyama Electric Light Co., Ltd.," and on February 25 the following year, 1898 (Meiji 31), a license to establish the company was granted by the Ministry of Agriculture and Commerce. Toyama Electric Light, thus founded, had capital of 100,000 yen. Kanaoka Matazaemon became the first president, and together with Micata Kōkichi, who became manager, he ran the company. Its shareholders were almost all residents of Toyama City or the adjacent Kaminiikawa District, making it a locally capitalized company.
After its founding, construction began around September 1898. The power station was built south of the urban area, in Ōaza Shio, Ōkubo Village, Kaminiikawa District (present-day Shio, Toyama City). This Ōkubo Power Station drew water from the Ōkubo irrigation canal, generated power by dropping the flowing water down a cliff, and discharged it into the main stream of the Jinzū River; it was a simple facility with no waterway tunnel, with an output of 120 kW. Because the design and supervision of the power station were entrusted to Kimura Komakichi, an engineer of Ōsaka Electric Light, it was equipped with a three-phase AC generator made by the American General Electric (GE), for which that company held exclusive domestic sales rights. A transmission line of just over 10 km was strung from the power station to the head office and distribution station in Hoshii-machi in the city, creating a system in which power was distributed from the distribution station to customers. And from April 2, 1899 (Meiji 32), Toyama Electric Light began operations.
On April 25, 1899, after the start of operations, an opening celebration was held at the high-class restaurant Hachiseirō. Electric rice-milling machines and an electric model of a marionette were displayed at the venue, and the model train was reportedly especially popular. The number of electric lights reached 957 by the end of the month, and three months later, in July, reached 1,510, consuming two-thirds of the generating capacity. Most installations were by shops, which reportedly vied to sign up for lighting because without electric lights they looked dark and shabby. However, on the night of August 12, four months after the start of operations, a great fire broke out that burned down 40% of Toyama City, and Toyama Electric Light lost its distribution equipment and most of its customers, suffering damages of 39,966 yen. To deal with this loss, the company reduced its capital from 100,000 yen to 60,000 yen. As the urban area was rebuilt, restoration proceeded, recovering to 1,300 lights by the end of the year, and exceeding 2,000 lights the following year, making the first dividend possible. In July 1903 (Meiji 36) it carried out its first capital increase, raising its capital to 90,000 yen.
=== Expansion after the Russo-Japanese War ===
On January 16, 1907 (Meiji 40), after the Russo-Japanese War, the company name was changed from Toyama Electric Light to Toyama Electric Co., Ltd. By this time the 120 kW generating capacity had become insufficient, so to raise expansion funds it increased its capital from 90,000 yen to 600,000 yen in January 1907 (Meiji 42), and in the first half of 1911 (Meiji 44) it carried out a further doubling of capital.
First, construction of thermal power stations that could be built in a short time was pushed forward, and the Ōkuda Power Station with an output of 110 kW was completed on land along the Jinzū River in Ōkuda Village, Kaminiikawa District, just north of Toyama City, starting generation on September 1, 1908 (Meiji 41). This power station used coal as fuel and a steam engine as the prime mover. In parallel with the thermal work, construction of a second hydroelectric station began in March 1908. The site was Ōaza Iodani, Honyū Village, Nei District (present-day Iodani, Toyama City), further south than the Ōkubo Power Station; it drew water from the Miyakawa River upstream on the Jinzū River and generated 1,425 kW using the head obtained from a waterway of just over 6.4 km. However, excavation of the waterway tunnel was difficult and the work was delayed, so this Iodani Power Station began operation on January 23, 1911 (Meiji 44).
With the completion of the Iodani Power Station, supply began to Higashi-Iwase-machi and Shinjō-machi outside the city and to Yao-machi in Nei District, and in March of the same year, with the completion of the Takatsuki transmission line, supply also began to Nishi-Mizuhashi-machi, Higashi-Mizuhashi-machi, Kamiichi-machi and Namerikawa-machi in Nakaniikawa District and to Uozu-machi (present-day Uozu City) in Shimoniikawa District. That year, the number of electric light customers expanded to 13,000 households, a fourfold increase over the previous year, and the number of installed lights to 25,000, a 3.5-fold increase. Furthermore, from May it also began supplying power to the Takaoka Electric Light power company in Takaoka City. That company, taking the start of receiving power as an opportunity, abolished its small thermal power station and temporarily became an operator specializing in distribution. It also supplied power from the start of operations to the Toyama Electric Tramway (the predecessor of the Toyama Chihō Railway Toyama Tram Line), Toyama Prefecture's first electric railway, which opened in September 1913 (Taishō 2).
In 1907, as the electric power business was expanding, Toyama Electric planned a city gas supply business and obtained permission from the Ministry of Agriculture and Commerce. However, because the Toyama City authorities viewed the gas business with concern, it could not obtain the city's permission to occupy roads and was unable to begin the business for a long time. In March 1912 (Meiji 45), when the gas business was spreading to other regional cities, the city finally granted permission to occupy roads. After the permission, work proceeded at a rapid pace to be in time for the One Prefecture and Eight Prefectures Joint Exposition held in the suburban Horikawa Village, and it opened on the day of the event, September 1, 1913 (Taishō 2).
The site of the gas works used the former site of the Ōkuda Power Station (present location of Nihonkai Gas's head office), which had been abolished in 1913, and two coal gas generators and one gas holder were installed there. According to reports just before the opening, the total length of gas pipes was 14.5 km. Gas was piped to 630 households in the city, with 1,308 gas light outlets in use and 552 outlets for heat (gas shichirin or gas rice cookers). Onlookers reportedly formed lines at the gas lamps on Sakurabashi Bridge, which were lit to coincide with the opening. Thereafter the gas business continued as a sideline of Toyama Electric, but since electricity was the core business there was no active investment in the gas business, and it merely saw a gradual increase in demand.
=== Supply to the Fushiki Port Industrial Zone ===
When the wartime boom brought on by World War I arrived, Toyama Electric quickly took measures to increase its generating capacity. The first was a reinforcement project to raise the output of the Ōkubo Power Station to 400 kW, completed in 1917 (Taishō 6). Next, in April 1918 (Taishō 7), the Hayatsuki No. 1 Power Station began operation. Its output was 1,024 kW, and it drew water from the Hayatsuki River. Subsequently, in June 1919 (Taishō 8), the Iodani No. 2 Power Station with an output of 7,110 kW (9,480 kW from November onward) was completed on the Jinzū River, and in December of the same year the Hayatsuki No. 2 Power Station with an output of 1,400 kW was completed on the Hayatsuki River. As a result of the additions, the generating capacity reached a total of 14,442 kW from five hydroelectric stations. Also, to raise development funds, its capital was increased to 3 million yen in 1917.
This active hydroelectric development by Toyama Electric was linked to attracting factories that consumed large amounts of electricity. A representative example was the Nippon Kōkan Electric Ironworks in Shinminato-machi (present-day Imizu City). It was built as a result of President Kanaoka Matazaemon and then-Managing Director Yamada Shōsaku working together with Shinminato-machi to persuade Asano Sōichirō, a native of the area; it began operation in September 1919 after the end of the war, operating an electric furnace with the cheap electricity supplied by Toyama Electric to produce pig iron (later converted to ferroalloy production). The electricity rate at the time of the June 1919 contract was 6 rin 5 mo per kilowatt-hour, about one-tenth of the rate for ordinary customers—very cheap.
In Fushiki-machi (present-day Takaoka City), which faces Shinminato across the Oyabe River, factories were also built one after another during the same period. One was Hokkai Denka Kōgyō, a carbide manufacturer that began operation in April 1918. This was attracted when Toyama Electric persuaded Yoshitomi Kiichi, an industrialist from Mitsui Bussan who planned to build a carbide plant. In 1919, the paper mill of Hokkai Kōgyō and the soda plant of Hokkai Sōda, in whose establishment that Yoshitomi was involved, also began operation in Fushiki-machi. In addition, Fushiki Seishi, a paperboard manufacturer established by Kansai industrialists, also appeared.
These four factories in the two towns of Fushiki and Shinminato—that is, the area around Fushiki Port—that appeared one after another from 1918 into the following year were all customers of Toyama Electric, and as of the second half of 1919 (November) it was supplying 1,197 kW to Nippon Kōkan, 345 kW to Hokkai Kōgyō, 300 kW to Fushiki Seishi, and 255 kW to Hokkai Sōda respectively. Among the four factories, the contracted power with Nippon Kōkan was 3,730 kW (5,000 horsepower), and the contract called for transmitting the full contracted amount from September 1919, but due to the expansion of general demand and the extension of the construction period of the Iodani No. 2 Power Station, there was little surplus supply capacity, and in reality it slipped to December of the same year. Toyama Electric had obtained approval to operate a chemical industry business concurrently in March 1917 during the war and had been producing potassium chloride in Horikawa Village from June of the same year, but with the expansion of power demand beyond expectations it became unable to operate and was forced to abolish its own factory.
During the war period, Toyama Electric's number of electric lights exceeded 50,000 in 1917 and reached 80,000 in 1920 (Taishō 9). In addition to supplying the factory zones, it also began supplying power in April 1918 to Himi Electric, a power company in Himi-machi, Himi District (present-day Himi City), and to Isurugi Electric, which distributed power to the western part of the prefecture.
=== Successive Acquisitions and Mergers ===
Entering the 1920s, Toyama Electric adopted a policy of merging small and medium-sized electric power operators and rapidly expanded its scale. In the process it extended its business territory not only into Toyama Prefecture but also into Ishikawa Prefecture, and so on December 26, 1928 (Shōwa 3) it changed its name to the publicly solicited new company name "Nihonkai Electric Co., Ltd."
The first business consolidation was the acquisition of the business of Nihon Denki Kōgyō in November 1921 (Taishō 10). That company was located in Nagaoka City, Niigata Prefecture, and was established in 1910. It built a hydroelectric station on the Katakai River flowing through eastern Toyama Prefecture and had been operating a carbide plant in Michishita Village, Shimoniikawa District (present-day Uozu City) since January 1912. Having been driven to close the plant by the postwar depression, its plant equipment and power station were taken over by Toyama Electric. As a result, the Katakai No. 1 Power Station was added to its own power stations, and the Katakai No. 2 Power Station with an output of 3,700 kW (7,400 kW from the following year), which Nihon Denki Kōgyō had been building, was also completed in August 1922 (Taishō 11).
Next, on June 1, 1926 (Taishō 15), it merged Himi Electric, a power company in Himi in the western part of the prefecture managed by Hirose Shizuyuki. That company had as its predecessor the Himi branch of Matsusaka Hydroelectric, headed by Saiga Tōkichi, and was formed by taking over the business of that branch, which had opened in July 1911, in September 1918. Since it had no power station of its own and, as mentioned above, received power from Toyama Electric, it desired a merger, and the merger was realized. Then on December 1 of the same year, it merged Noto Electric, a power company on the Noto Peninsula north of Himi. That company was established in January 1920 by combining four operators located in Nanao, Shio and Takahama in the central part of the peninsula and Wajima in the north. In the year before the merger it had also merged an operator in Hakui. As a result of merging Noto Electric, Toyama Electric established a Noto branch in Nanao-machi. Also, at the same time, Takaoka Electric Light in the same Toyama Prefecture merged Noto's Nōshū Electric, so the Noto Peninsula became an area where the supply areas of Toyama Electric and Takaoka Electric Light were intertwined.
On June 1, 1928, it merged Chūetsu Suiden. That company had as its predecessor Chūetsu Denki Kōgyō, established in September 1918 for the purpose of developing the Kumano River, and after entering the 1920s it consolidated six operators in Toyama Prefecture and further expanded its business aggressively, including developing hydroelectric power on the Oguchi River of the Jōganji River system. In February 1927 it began supplying 1,000 kW to the Nihon Sōda Toyama Plant (closed in 1942) built in Yamamuro Village, Kaminiikawa District, on the outskirts of Toyama City, posing a threat to Toyama Electric, which was based in Toyama. However, when the president who had promoted the aggressive policy died suddenly in May of that year, it soon chose to merge with Toyama Electric.
Following the merger of Chūetsu Suiden, in December 1928 it brought Komatsu Electric of Ishikawa Prefecture under its umbrella. That company was a power company based in Komatsu-machi, Nomi District (present-day Komatsu City), but it also operated a branch in Tomari-machi, Shimoniikawa District (present-day Asahi-machi) in eastern Toyama Prefecture. Because of a plan to transmit surplus power from the Ishikawa side to the Tomari district using Toyama Electric's transmission lines, it came under Toyama Electric's umbrella when the latter bought its shares.
Through this series of mergers, the number of electric lights, which had exceeded 100,000 in 1922, doubled to 250,000 in 1927, five years later, and reached 300,000 the following year, 1928. Meanwhile, with the increase in power supply, power rate revenue exceeded electric light rate revenue from 1920, and the gap continued to widen thereafter. Also, through the series of mergers its capital reached 21.35 million yen, and after the renaming to Nihonkai Electric, a disguised capital increase was carried out in the form of newly establishing "Dai-ni Nihonkai Electric Co., Ltd." and absorbing it. This second company was founded on November 12, 1929 (Shōwa 4). Its capital was 11.15 million yen, contributed by shareholders and employees of Nihonkai Electric. On February 1, 1930 (Shōwa 5), the second company was merged into Nihonkai Electric, and Nihonkai Electric's capital became 32.5 million yen. During this period, in June 1929, Kanaoka Matazaemon, the president since the founding, died, and Yamada Shōsaku took office as his successor.
=== The Toyama Electric Dispute ===
While Toyama Electric expanded its scale and developed into Nihonkai Electric, a dispute originating in a movement to lower electricity rates, the so-called "electricity dispute," broke out in Toyama Prefecture. The electricity dispute in Toyama is regarded as the first of its kind, which spread nationwide under the recession of the late 1920s.
The origin of the electricity rate reduction movement may date back earlier, but directly it is thought to have been triggered by a movement that began in 1927 (Shōwa 2) in the Nakaniikawa and Shimoniikawa districts of eastern Toyama Prefecture. First, in September, a rate reduction movement began at the chambers of commerce and industry of Higashi-Mizuhashi-machi and Namerikawa-machi in Nakaniikawa District. In response, from October the Nakaniikawa/Shimoniikawa Union Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the parent body of the chambers, negotiated rate reductions with Toyama Electric, but no reduction was realized. On October 10, a residents' meeting was held in Mikkaichi-machi, Shimoniikawa District, and adopted a declaration demanding a 35% reduction per electric light, a halving of the flat-rate power charge, and reductions or abolition of other incidental charges. Entering November, the movement spread to Nishi-Mizuhashi-machi and Higashi-Iwase-machi in Kaminiikawa District, and by early December, electricity rate reduction promotion leagues were formed in each of the five towns of Higashi-Iwase, Nishi-Mizuhashi, Higashi-Mizuhashi, Namerikawa and Mikkaichi.
On December 16, 1927, the promotion leagues of the five towns formed the Toyama Electric Company Area Electricity Rate Reduction Promotion League Federation. Surrounding towns and villages later joined the federation. The federation held a speech meeting on the 22nd, then held a demonstration march from Toyama Station to Toyama Electric's head office, directly appealed to the president for a reduction at the head office, and then conducted petitioning activities at the prefectural office. The federation demanded a 35% reduction in electric light rates and a halving of the metered electric light rate and the flat-rate power charge, but negotiations with the company broke down, and it proceeded to a fee non-payment movement as the next step.
On May 1, 1928 (Shōwa 3), Toyama Electric implemented a partial rate reduction, and on the 15th notified non-payers that power transmission would be stopped unless payment was made by the 17th. On the 17th it actually carried out blackouts in Higashi-Mizuhashi-machi, Nishi-Mizuhashi-machi and Mikkaichi-machi, but these were lifted after one day by order of the Ministry of Home Affairs. As the situation became more serious, a mediation committee was organized by the prefectural authorities, town and village mayors and local influential figures, and on July 11 it presented to both the company and the federation a mediation proposal consisting of a 15.25% reduction in electricity rates and service improvements, but both sides rejected it. Then on the 26th, disconnection was carried out for 181 non-paying households. Against this measure by the company, a blackout movement arose in the five towns of Higashi-Iwase, Nishi-Mizuhashi, Higashi-Mizuhashi, Namerikawa and Mikkaichi in which the entire towns turned off their lights and returned the bulbs provided by the company, and thereafter electric lights disappeared from the five towns for one month.
However, as the blackout movement dragged on, the federation's ranks became disordered, and in August there was a succession of withdrawals from the blackout movement. On August 20, both the company and the federation agreed to the rate reduction from September 1 (including a 10-sen reduction in the flat-rate electric light charge) presented by Prefectural Governor Shirane Takesuke. The electricity dispute was entirely concluded when Namerikawa-machi, which had continued activities demanding municipalization of the electric power business, shelved municipalization and restored lighting on September 15. However, similar disputes spread throughout Japan and also spread to the service areas of other companies within Toyama Prefecture, and at the peak in 1930, as many as 162 rate reduction movements occurred in 38 prefectures.
=== Kurobe River Electric Power and Kokusan Hiryō ===
In April 1929 and November 1931 (Shōwa 6), the Oguchi River No. 2 Power Station (output 3,100 kW) and the Oguchi River No. 3 Power Station (output 7,150 kW) began operation on the Oguchi River, a tributary of the Jōganji River. These power stations are located upstream of the existing Oguchi River No. 1 Power Station. The Oguchi River No. 3 Power Station draws water from the Sukenobu Dam at the very top of the Oguchi River and has a large reservoir. Accordingly, in principle it stopped generating during the abundant-water seasons of spring and autumn and concentrated on storing water, and it was operated as a supplementary power station like the thermal power stations of the time, discharging water and generating mainly during the dry seasons of summer and winter. Also, because the regulating reservoir of the Oguchi River No. 2 Power Station is located just downstream of the power station, pumping equipment to return the water of the regulating reservoir to the Sukenobu Dam was added in May 1934 (Shōwa 9), making possible pumped-storage generation that effectively used surplus power.
In parallel with its own development, in September 1929 Nihonkai Electric brought under its umbrella Kurobe River Electric Power, which undertook power source development on the Kurobe River in eastern Toyama Prefecture. That company was established in October 1923 as an affiliate of Kawakita Denki Kigyōsha, headed by Kawakita Hideo. It opened in June 1926 and transmitted power to Nihonkai Electric and to Denki Kagaku Kōgyō (present-day Denka), which had a plant in Niigata Prefecture. Because Kawakita Denki Kigyōsha fell into management difficulties, President Kawakita Hideo brought a buyout offer, which Nihonkai Electric accepted, making it an affiliate. Its power stations were the No. 1 Power Station (output 7,760 kW), the No. 2 Power Station (output 6,330 kW) and the No. 3 Power Station (output 3,700 kW) added in 1929.
One of Kurobe River Electric Power's supply destinations, Denki Kagaku Kōgyō's Ōmi Plant, was also a customer of Nihonkai Electric, which had been transmitting power to it since August 1922. As of the end of June 1930, the supplied power was 8,000 kW from Nihonkai Electric and 17,000 kW from Kurobe River Electric Power. The rates were also cheap: for the Nihonkai Electric portion and the first-term contract portion of Kurobe River Electric Power, 1 sen 2 rin 5 mo per kWh for scheduled power and 8 rin for unscheduled power, and for the second-term contract portion of Kurobe River Electric Power, 8 rin 5 mo for scheduled and 7 rin 7 mo for unscheduled. However, Denki Kagaku Kōgyō fell into extreme management difficulties due to the collapse of ammonium sulfate prices in the early 1930s, and ultimately fell into a situation where it could not pay unless the rate was 3 rin or less per kWh. In July 1932 (Shōwa 7), as a result of direct negotiations between Denki Kagaku Kōgyō Chairman Fujiwara Ginjirō and Nihonkai Electric President Yamada Shōsaku, a support measure was agreed to the effect that Denki Kagaku Kōgyō would provide its own power stations to Kurobe River Electric Power to cancel its unpaid charges, and after the provision it would, in principle, receive only unscheduled power at 3 rin per kWh (though rising in line with future increases in ammonium sulfate prices). In May 1933 (Shōwa 8), two of Denki Kagaku Kōgyō's own power stations were contributed in kind to Kurobe River Electric Power, and that company became a power company with capital of 18 million yen, half-funded by Nihonkai Electric.
Alongside Kurobe River Electric Power, one of Nihonkai Electric's main affiliated companies was Kokusan Hiryō Co., Ltd. (Domestic Fertilizer). That company was founded on April 19, 1929 with capital of 1 million yen through cooperation between Fujiyama Tsuneichi, then a managing director of Denki Kagaku Kōgyō, and Nihonkai Electric. It rebuilt a plant on the former site of Nihon Denki Kōgyō in Michishita Village, Shimoniikawa District, where Nihonkai Electric owned land, installed an electric furnace using the Fujiyama-type electrode devised by Fujiyama, and began manufacturing carbide and calcium cyanamide from February 1930 using power supplied by Nihonkai Electric. However, the operation of the new electric furnace was technically difficult and calcium cyanamide production was also sluggish, so funds soon ran out and operation was suspended. As a result, in August of the same year Fujiyama and others stepped down and Nihonkai Electric took over the cleanup. The plant was closed, but employees organized the "Uozu Carbide Manufacturing Cooperative" and resumed operation in October 1931. When carbide prices recovered thereafter, Nihonkai Electric decided to revive the plant to make use of surplus power, and in April 1933 it returned the plant to the management of Kokusan Hiryō. Thereafter equipment improvements were pushed forward, and on June 22, 1934 it established Dai-ni Kokusan Hiryō, and with effect from November 22 it carried out a reorganization in the form of substantially reducing the capital of the first Kokusan Hiryō and having it absorbed to become the second-generation Kokusan Hiryō.
On October 8, 1935 (Shōwa 10), Nihon Carbide Kōgyō was established by Tōyō Chisso Kōgyō as a new company for a synthetic benzene business that synthesized benzene from acetylene. That company, in order to hurry the business, adopted a policy of acquiring an existing plant rather than building a new one, and after surveying the whole country it judged suitable the Kokusan Hiryō plant that was under Nihonkai Electric's umbrella and received its cheap power. Nihonkai Electric, which was also struggling with the plant's management, accepted Tōyō Chisso Kōgyō's acquisition proposal, and as a result, with effect from February 1, 1936 (Shōwa 11), Kokusan Hiryō was merged into Nihon Carbide Kōgyō, and the Michishita Village plant became Nihon Carbide Kōgyō's Uozu Plant.
=== Supply to the Toyama Port Industrial Zone ===
As of the end of November 1938 (Shōwa 13), the supply results were 374,418 installed electric lights, 8,137 kW of small-lot power sales, and 139,957 kW of large-lot power sales. Throughout the 1930s the growth in the number of installed electric lights was slow, and electric light rate revenue remained almost flat. On the other hand, power supply, centered on large-lot supply, grew greatly, and power rate revenue increased steadily accordingly, reaching four times the scale of electric light rate revenue in the second-half settlement of accounts for 1938. Large-lot supply centered on heavy and chemical industry, and although the figures are as of the end of 1939, the large-lot factory customers (those listed as supplied with 3,000 kW or more) were as follows.
Of these, the three plants—Nichiman Aluminium, Nihon Sōda's Iwase Plant, and Tōyō Sōda's Toyama Plant—were plants that advanced along Toyama Port or the Fugan Canal. The first to advance into this area was Tōyō Sōda's Toyama Plant (initially the Dai-ni Tōyō Sōda Higashi-Iwase Plant), affiliated with Hodogaya Chemical Industry, which began producing metallic sodium and sodium cyanide in 1930. It is said that Nihonkai Electric was involved in the plant's advance.
The largest large-lot customer, Nichiman Aluminium, was founded in October 1933. After building a temporary plant for testing in December, it built the main plant and began alumina production from May 1935 and aluminum refining from July. In building the plant, Nichiman Aluminium sounded out Toyama Prefecture, which operated a prefectural power generation business, about the huge amount of power supply needed for aluminum refining. The prefecture, judging that it matched its factory attraction policy, accepted the request and decided to transmit power from prefectural power stations via Nihonkai Electric; based on this, Nihonkai Electric concluded a contract with Nichiman Aluminium to supply constant power of 32,900 kW at 5 rin 7 mo 8 shi per kWh. In June 1936, after the plant began operation, the Aimoto Power Station (output 29,700 kW), which the prefecture had built on the Kurobe River to supply Nichiman Aluminium, began operation.
Nihon Sōda had been a customer since the Chūetsu Suiden era, and in October 1936 it built a new ferroalloy plant, the Iwase Plant, in Higashi-Iwase-machi. In addition, Nissō Jin'ken Pulp (present-day Kōjin), under Nihon Sōda's umbrella, advanced to present-day Kōjin-machi, Toyama City along the Fugan Canal and set up the Toyama Plant in June 1938. When Nissō Jin'ken Pulp advanced, Nihonkai Electric newly established the Toyama Thermal Power Station with an output of 10,000 kW on September 30 of the same year, mainly to supply the steam used by that company in manufacturing rayon pulp.
Following the above Toyama Thermal Power Station, on December 3, 1939 (Shōwa 14) and January 9 of the following year, 1940 (Shōwa 15), the Katakai No. 3 Power Station (output 2,900 kW) and the Katakai No. 4 Power Station (output 15,500 kW) began operation on the Katakai River respectively. With the completion of both power stations, the company had 20 hydroelectric and 1 thermal power stations, with a total output of 72,340 kW. On the other hand, received power included 59,700 kW from Toyama Prefecture's Magawa and Aimoto power stations and 27,000 kW from Kurobe River Electric Power, totaling 99,359 kW from 8 operators (interchange power not included in the calculation), and the total of generation and reception was 171,699 kW.
In the latter half of the 1930s there were also developments in the sideline city gas business within Toyama City; large-lot customers such as the restaurant in the Toyama Electric Building, the Daiwa Department Store and the prefectural office joined, and moreover supply to munitions factories was expected to increase with the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War, so in December 1937 a No. 2 gas holder was newly installed at the works. Then in January 1939 one gas furnace was added to supply Fujikoshi Steel Industry. The annual gas sales volume for fiscal 1938 was 1,075,663 cubic meters.
=== Participation in Hokuriku Gōdō Electric ===
==== Prior Consolidation of Small and Medium Operators ====
Amid the trend toward state control of electric power in the latter half of the 1930s that culminated in the establishment of Nihon Hassōden in 1939, the consolidation of small-scale operators flourished nationwide. Nihonkai Electric likewise took over businesses from each company in the order of Yamazaki Suiden on May 23, 1938; Ōiwa Electric on September 30; Nozumi River Hydroelectric and Kaminakajima Hydroelectric in February of the following year, 1939; Nōetsu Electric in October; and Otagawa Bussan on March 28, 1940.
Yamazaki Suiden Co., Ltd.
Established in February 1920. In December of the same year it opened with only Yamazaki Village, Shimoniikawa District (present-day Asahi-machi) as its supply area.
Ōiwa Electric Co., Ltd.
Its predecessor was Ōiwayama Electric Light Gōshi Kaisha, which opened in Ōiwa Village, Nakaniikawa District (present-day Kamiichi-machi) in August 1912. In July 1913 it was reorganized into Ōiwa Electric Co., Ltd. with capital of 100,000 yen, and it built the Ōiwa Power Station in 1915 and the Takihashi Power Station in 1919. It expanded its supply area beyond Ōiwa Village into parts of Nakaniikawa and Kaminiikawa districts. In 1926 it came under the umbrella of Takaoka Electric Light. However, because of the geographical relationship of its supply area, it was integrated into Nihonkai Electric rather than Takaoka Electric Light.
Nozumi River Hydroelectric Co., Ltd.
Established in August 1919. In September 1920 it built the Ryōshigahara Power Station on the Nozumi River and opened with the two villages of Nozumi and Nippo (present-day Toyama City) in the mountainous area of Nei District as its supply area. Its electric light supply was small-scale, and selling power to other power companies such as Nihonkai Electric was its main business.
Kaminakajima Hydroelectric Co., Ltd.
Established in January 1921. It was a small operator in Kaminakajima Village, Shimoniikawa District (present-day Uozu City), and opened in July of the same year.
Nōetsu Electric Co., Ltd.
It was established in 1922 as "Yasui Electric Industry Co., Ltd." and renamed Nōetsu Electric in 1924. In November 1923 it opened with an area straddling Himi District, Toyama Prefecture and Kashima District, Ishikawa Prefecture as its supply area.
Otagawa Bussan Co., Ltd.
A cotton and textile manufacturing company established in March 1920. From 1924 it began electric light supply in Otagawa Village, Nei District (present-day Toyama City).
Apart from these small operators, in January 1938 Nihonkai Electric bought shares of Tateyama Hydroelectric from the industry giant Daidō Electric Power. As a result of the acquisition, Yamada Shōsaku also became president of that company. That company had three hydroelectric stations on the Hayatsuki River and supplied power to plants located at Fushiki Port and to Nihonkai Electric, Takaoka Electric Light and others.
==== From Hokuriku Gōdō Electric to Hokuriku Haiden ====
On April 1, 1939, Nihon Hassōden, a national-policy electric power company, was established by receiving in-kind contributions of major power facilities from operators nationwide, but at this stage none of the power companies based in the Hokuriku region, including Nihonkai Electric, contributed facilities to Nihon Hassōden. Also, at the time of its establishment, Nihon Hassōden's main business was to purchase the power generated by major hydroelectric stations and supply it to electric power operators, but no power transmission/reception relationship arose with Nihonkai Electric.
In 1940 (Shōwa 15), a movement arose aiming to strengthen Nihon Hassōden's structure and to consolidate and bring under state control the power distribution business (the second phase of state control of electric power). In response to this movement, Yamada Shōsaku, who led Nihonkai Electric, set forth a policy of rapidly advancing voluntary consolidation and business rationalization, and brought the matter to Kanno Den'emon, president of Takaoka Electric Light. Kanno was reluctant about the consolidation because of disagreement of opinion within Takaoka Electric Light, but he reportedly became positive about it through the enthusiastic persuasion of Yamada and of Nishi Taizō, the manager who had moved over from Nihonkai Electric. Because Takaoka Electric Light showed its intention to participate in the combination, the Nagoya Communications Bureau also came to encourage the consolidation of businesses in the three Hokuriku prefectures. Preparations for the combination began at the end of 1940, and on March 10 of the following year, 1941 (Shōwa 16), they advanced to the signing of the merger contract.
The power companies participating in the combination were the six of Nihonkai Electric, Takaoka Electric Light, Kanazawa Electric Tramway, Komatsu Electric, Daishōjigawa Suiden and Echizen Electric, plus six affiliated companies of each including Tateyama Hydroelectric, for a total of 12 companies. This did not include Kyōto Electric Light, which supplied most of Fukui Prefecture, but it covered the main private operators of the three Hokuriku prefectures. And on August 1 of the same year the combination of the 12 companies was formed, and the new company Hokuriku Gōdō Electric Co., Ltd. was founded. With this consolidation by new establishment, the 12 old companies including Nihonkai Electric were dissolved. Nihonkai Electric had set its capital at 50 million yen through a capital increase in December 1939, and its paid-in capital at the time of the merger was 36,875,000 yen, the largest among the 12 consolidated companies. The share exchange ratio with the new company was adjusted to one-to-one.
At the end of August 1941, shortly after the establishment of Hokuriku Gōdō Electric, the Electricity Distribution Control Ordinance, which incorporated the consolidation of distribution by national-policy distribution companies as part of the second phase of state control of electric power, came into force. In the distribution control, the plan of dividing the whole country into eight blocks and consolidating distribution businesses by region was initially dominant, and the three Hokuriku prefectures were to be included in the Chūbu block together with the Tōkai region. However, Yamada Shōsaku, who also served as president of Hokuriku Gōdō Electric, vigorously carried out a movement for the independence of the three Hokuriku prefectures, and shortly after the new company's founding he got it recognized that the three Hokuriku prefectures would be a separate block from the Tōkai region. Then in September, an order to establish the national-policy distribution company "Hokuriku Haiden" was issued to Hokuriku Gōdō Electric, Kyōto Electric Light, Nihon Denryoku, and the city of Kanazawa, which operated a municipal supply business, and on April 1 of the following year, 1942 (Shōwa 17), Hokuriku Haiden was established with Toyama and Ishikawa prefectures and the area of Fukui Prefecture excluding the Wakasa region as its distribution area.

=== Toyama Electric Building ===
In 1935, in the central part of Toyama City, the land-reclamation work on the abandoned Jinzū River channel that had divided the urban area north-south was completed. Toyama Prefecture, which carried out the work, when selling the developed land, sounded out Nihonkai Electric, which was considering building a new company building. In response, the company purchased about 3,000 tsubo of the reclaimed land and established a new company, "Toyama Electric Building Co., Ltd.," in February 1936 (Shōwa 11) to operate and manage the new building. Its capital at establishment was 1 million yen, and of the total 20,000 shares, 13,250 were held by Nihonkai Electric, while others investing included Kurobe River Electric Power, Komatsu Electric and Takaoka Electric Light, as well as the central companies Daidō Electric Power and Nihon Denryoku (Niden Securities), and Nihon Carbide Kōgyō, Nichiman Aluminium, Denki Kagaku Kōgyō, Nisshin Spinning and Dai-Nihon Artificial Fertilizer, which had plants around Toyama Prefecture.
The Toyama Electric Building was completed on March 31, 1936. Consisting of one basement floor and five above-ground floors, it housed Nihonkai Electric and Kurobe River Electric Power, and on the fourth floor a hotel and restaurant and the Toyama Social Club were established, while on the fifth floor a large hall was established.
=== Nittō Bibai Coal Mine ===
In 1937, a proposal was brought to Nihonkai Electric, which was studying procurement methods for the coal used at the Toyama Thermal Power Station, to develop the mining area held by Yamaichi Securities and others at Bibai (Bibai Coal Mine) in Hokkaido. After investigation, Nihonkai Electric decided to undertake the development and established Nittō Bibai Coal Mine Co., Ltd. holding a majority of the shares. Coal extraction was 3,000 tons per month, half of which was consumed in-house at thermal power stations and the like, with the rest sold to the general public.
=== Disposal of Shares Held ===
At the establishment of Hokuriku Gōdō Electric in August 1941, while setting the share exchange ratio between Hokuriku Gōdō Electric and Nihonkai Electric at one-to-one, a policy was adopted not to bring Nihonkai Electric's sideline gas business and affiliated company shares into Hokuriku Gōdō Electric, and special measures were taken.
At the establishment of Hokuriku Gōdō Electric, the assets scheduled for separation were for the time being inherited by that company, and an amount of compensation corresponding to that value (20% of the paid-in amount) was paid to the shareholders of the old Nihonkai Electric. The shareholders who received it applied that compensation directly to the payment for shares for the establishment of "Nihonkai Sangyō Co., Ltd." This new company was founded on October 1, 1941, and with the paid-in money it bought from Hokuriku Gōdō Electric the gas business and its related assets as well as the affiliated company shares held by the old Nihonkai Electric, assets totaling 7,375,000 yen. The shares taken over by Nihonkai Sangyō included Hokuriku Gōdō Electric shares (former Komatsu Electric and Tateyama Hydroelectric shares) as well as shares of Toyama Electric Building, Nittō Bibai Coal Mine, Kureha Boseki, Nihon Carbide Kōgyō, Toyama Electric Railway, Nichiman Aluminium, Nissō Jin'ken Pulp and Hokkai Denka Kōgyō.
Nihonkai Sangyō lost its function within one year of its founding due to the strengthening of dividend controls and was dissolved on October 15, 1942 (Shōwa 17). Only the gas business was inherited by the newly established Nihonkai Gas (present-day Nihonkai Gas).
